lessonTitle: Colorectal and Upper Gastrointestinal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Treatment

blocks.text: A 64-year-old retired bus driver visits his GP because he has felt tired for four months and climbing stairs leaves him breathless. His haemoglobin is 91 g/L with a mean cell volume of 69 fL, and he has no bleeding he has noticed. The blood count has told you there is a bleeding source in his gut until proven otherwise, and the most likely site is the right colon.

blocks.markdown: Colorectal cancer is predominantly adenocarcinoma arising from adenomatous polyps through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence over years. Symptoms depend on site. **Right-sided (caecum, ascending colon) tumours** have a wide lumen and liquid stool, so they present late with iron-deficiency anaemia, fatigue, weight loss or a palpable right iliac fossa mass. **Left-sided tumours** and **rectal tumours** present earlier with altered bowel habit, rectal bleeding, tenesmus (a sense of incomplete evacuation), obstruction or a palpable rectal mass. Some present as emergencies with obstruction or perforation.

blocks.title: Red-flag symptoms and the urgent pathway
blocks.text: UK guidance (NICE NG12) advises urgent assessment for suspected colorectal cancer in adults with, for example, unexplained rectal bleeding aged 50 or over, a change in bowel habit or iron-deficiency anaemia aged 60 or over, or a rectal or abdominal mass. A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) is used to triage symptomatic patients without an obvious mass; a positive result (about 10 micrograms haemoglobin per gram of faeces or more) leads to urgent referral. Thresholds change with guidance updates.

blocks.markdown: **Colonoscopy** is the reference investigation: it visualises the entire colon, allows biopsy for histology, removal of polyps (polypectomy), tattooing of tumours for surgery and detection of synchronous lesions (a second tumour in about 3 to 5%). CT colonography is an alternative when colonoscopy is incomplete or unsuitable. A rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy suffices for a low rectal lesion but misses proximal disease. Once a cancer is confirmed, staging uses CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (liver and lung metastases), MRI of the pelvis for rectal tumours (local extent, circumferential margin, nodes), and a baseline carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) used for follow-up, not for diagnosis.

blocks.caption: TNM staging of colorectal cancer (simplified, AJCC/UICC)
rows: Local excision may be adequate for selected early lesions
Through muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissue
Penetrates visceral peritoneum / invades adjacent organs
1 to 3 / 4 or more regional nodes positive
At least 12 nodes should be examined

blocks.title: Assigning TNM and stage group
blocks.prompt: A resected sigmoid cancer invades through the muscularis propria into pericolic fat without breaching the peritoneal surface. Of 16 lymph nodes examined, 2 contain tumour. CT shows no distant disease. Give the TNM category and the stage group, using stage I = T1-2 N0, II = T3-4 N0, III = any T with N+, IV = M1.

steps.text: Invasion through muscularis propria into pericolic tissue without peritoneal breach is T3.
Two positive nodes falls within 1 to 3 positive nodes, therefore N1. The sample of 16 nodes exceeds the minimum of 12, so staging is adequate.
Any T with positive nodes is stage III.

blocks.answer: pT3 N1 M0, stage III colon cancer.

blocks.markdown: **The multidisciplinary team (MDT)** brings together the colorectal surgeon, oncologist, radiologist, histopathologist, specialist nurse and, as needed, gastroenterologist and palliative care. It reviews imaging and pathology, confirms stage, matches treatment to patient fitness and preference, and reduces variation in care. Outcomes are better in centres where all cancers are discussed at an MDT.

**Curative resection.** The principle is removal of the tumour with clear margins together with its lymphovascular drainage, with the vessels ligated at their origin (complete mesocolic excision for colon). For rectal cancer, **total mesorectal excision (TME)** removes the rectum with its surrounding mesorectal fat envelope along the embryological plane, reducing local recurrence and a positive circumferential margin. Anastomosis may be protected by a temporary stoma. **Adjuvant chemotherapy** (usually a fluoropyrimidine, often with oxaliplatin) is offered for stage III and high-risk stage II colon cancer. **Neoadjuvant** radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy is used for locally advanced rectal cancer to shrink tumour and reduce recurrence.

blocks.latex: \text{Lymph node ratio} = \frac{\text{number of positive nodes}}{\text{number of nodes examined}}
blocks.caption: A prognostic indicator; higher ratios predict worse outcomes.

blocks.title: Calculating the lymph node ratio
blocks.prompt: A rectal cancer specimen contains 20 lymph nodes, of which 5 are positive. Find the N category (N1 = 1 to 3 positive, N2 = 4 or more) and the lymph node ratio.

steps.text: 5 positive nodes is 4 or more, so N2.

blocks.markdown: **Upper gastrointestinal cancer.** Oesophageal cancer (squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma, the latter linked to Barrett's oesophagus and reflux) presents with progressive dysphagia, first for solids then liquids, with weight loss; dysphagia at any age warrants urgent upper endoscopy with biopsy. Gastric cancer presents with weight loss, early satiety, epigastric pain, vomiting or anaemia. Staging combines CT, endoscopic ultrasound for depth and nodes, and often PET-CT and laparoscopy. Treatment of potentially curable disease is multimodal: perioperative or neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy or gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy.

blocks.caption: Which test for which question in GI cancer
rows: Is there a colonic tumour or polyp, and what is its histology?
Are there liver or lung metastases?
How deep does a rectal tumour go, and is the circumferential margin threatened?
Depth of oesophageal tumour and nodes?
Is there occult distant disease in oesophageal cancer?

blocks.title: Curative intent needs three things
blocks.text: Complete (R0) resection with clear margins, adequate lymph node clearance and staging-guided adjuvant or neoadjuvant therapy. Treatment intent is decided at the MDT after staging and assessment of fitness.

points: Right-sided colon cancer often presents with iron-deficiency anaemia; left-sided and rectal cancers with altered bowel habit, bleeding and obstruction.
Colonoscopy with biopsy is the key diagnostic test; CT stages distant disease and MRI stages rectal cancer locally.
TNM staging relies on depth of invasion, nodal involvement and metastases; at least 12 nodes should be examined, and the MDT directs care.

Curative resection uses en-bloc excision with lymphatic clearance (TME in rectum), with adjuvant chemotherapy for stage III or high-risk disease and neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal and upper GI cancers.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had a change in bowel habit towards looser stools for 10 weeks. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Urgent investigation for suspected colorectal cancer, such as FIT-triaged referral and colonoscopy
Reassure that this is normal ageing
Prescribe laxatives and review in a year

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent investigation for suspected colorectal cancer, such as FIT-triaged referral and colonoscopy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent change in bowel habit at 60 or over is a red flag.
distractorRationale.b: A persistent change is not normal ageing.
distractorRationale.c: Treating symptoms without a diagnosis delays cancer detection.
distractorRationale.d: Diet alone is not adequate in a red-flag patient.

questions.explanation: A persistent change in bowel habit in someone aged 60 or over meets urgent referral criteria. Early colonoscopy detects cancer at a more treatable stage.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man presents with fatigue and Hb 88 g/L with microcytosis, but normal bowel habit. A mass is palpable in the right iliac fossa. Which is the most likely site of the tumour?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: large lumen, liquid stool and occult bleeding give anaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Low rectal cancer gives bleeding, tenesmus and altered habit.
distractorRationale.c: Sigmoid cancers more often alter habit or obstruct.
distractorRationale.d: Anal canal tumours present with pain, bleeding or lump.

questions.explanation: Right-sided tumours bleed slowly and occultly, so iron-deficiency anaemia and a mass are typical, while bowel habit remains normal because the lumen is wide. Left-sided tumours obstruct earlier.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has progressive dysphagia for solids over 2 months and has lost 7 kg. Biopsy at endoscopy shows adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus. Which investigation best assesses the depth of tumour invasion and regional nodes?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: EUS images the wall layers and adjacent nodes.
distractorRationale.b: A chest film cannot stage local invasion.
distractorRationale.c: CEA is not a staging test.
distractorRationale.d: Barium shows a stricture but not depth or nodes.

questions.explanation: Endoscopic ultrasound visualises the layers of the oesophageal wall and peri-oesophageal nodes, defining T and N categories. CT and PET-CT complement it by looking for distant disease.

questions.stem: A resected colon cancer invades into the muscularis propria but not beyond it. There are 0 positive nodes of 14, and no metastases. What is the pathological stage?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: muscularis propria invasion without nodes is T2, stage I.
distractorRationale.b: T3 requires invasion through the muscularis propria.
distractorRationale.d: T1 is limited to the submucosa.

questions.explanation: Invasion into but not through the muscularis propria defines T2. With no nodal or distant disease the stage is I, so surgery alone is usually curative.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer?

options.text: Sharp dissection along the embryological plane to remove the rectum with its intact mesorectal fat envelope and nodes, reducing local recurrence
Blunt finger dissection removing only the rectal wall
Local excision of the tumour with a 1 mm margin in all cases
Removal of the whole colon and rectum

questions.correctOptionText: Sharp dissection along the embryological plane to remove the rectum with its intact mesorectal fat envelope and nodes, reducing local recurrence

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the mesorectal envelope contains lymphatic spread and tumour deposits.
distractorRationale.b: This would leave nodes and cause recurrence.
distractorRationale.c: Local excision is for selected early tumours, not standard.
distractorRationale.d: Panproctocolectomy is for other indications such as polyposis.

questions.explanation: The rectum and mesorectum form a fascial envelope that holds the lymphatics, so removing it intact lowers positive margin and recurrence rates. TME is the standard curative operation for mid and low rectal cancer.

questions.stem: Adjuvant chemotherapy after curative resection is considered for stage III colon cancer.
questions.explanation: Node-positive disease carries a substantial risk of micrometastatic recurrence, and adjuvant chemotherapy reduces that risk. Fitness and preferences are weighed at the MDT.

questions.stem: A sigmoid colectomy specimen contains 18 lymph nodes, 3 of which are positive for tumour. Calculate the lymph node ratio (a unitless fraction, to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: The ratio is positive nodes divided by nodes examined, 3 / 18 = 0.1667, or about 0.17. Three positive nodes also corresponds to N1.

questions.stem: Describe the role of the multidisciplinary team in managing a patient with newly diagnosed rectal cancer.
markingGuide: Membership: surgeon, oncologist, radiologist, pathologist, specialist nurse, others
Review of MRI pelvis and CT for local and distant stage
Decide treatment: neoadjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, surgery, adjuvant therapy
Consider fitness, comorbidity and patient preferences
Improves consistency and outcomes; plan follow-up
questions.explanation: The MDT integrates staging, histology and patient factors to produce a single evidence-based plan. This reduces variation and improves survival.

questions.stem: Outline the principles of curative surgery for colon cancer and the role of adjuvant therapy, using stage to justify your answer.
markingGuide: En-bloc resection of tumour with adequate longitudinal margins
Removal of lymphovascular pedicle at its origin, at least 12 nodes
Primary anastomosis, with or without stoma
Stage I: surgery alone; stage II: consider adjuvant if high-risk features
Stage III: adjuvant chemotherapy, typically fluoropyrimidine with oxaliplatin
Stage IV: MDT decides on resection of metastases and systemic therapy
questions.explanation: Cure depends on removing all macroscopic disease along with the draining nodes, and treating micrometastases when node-positive. Stage determines the risk of relapse and the benefit of chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had 3 months of bright red rectal bleeding mixed with stool and a sense of incomplete evacuation. Explain the likely diagnosis, how you would investigate, and why colonoscopy is preferred as the reference test.
markingGuide: Suspect rectal or distal colorectal cancer (bleeding with tenesmus)
Digital rectal examination, bloods including FBC
Urgent colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy
Colonoscopy enables direct visualisation, biopsy and polypectomy
Detects synchronous lesions in the rest of the colon
Staging after diagnosis with CT and MRI pelvis
questions.explanation: Bleeding with tenesmus points to a rectal lesion, which needs tissue confirmation. Colonoscopy both diagnoses and treats polyps, and sees the whole colon, unlike indirect radiological tests.
